copies.headline: Adam Built A Wideout Room And Waited On Quarterback
copies.body:
The plan was obvious in hindsight, which is how you know it was good. Jaxon Smith-Njigba at 1.07 as the WR3 off the board, Chris Olave at 3.31 as WR10, Rome Odunze in the fifth — that's three receivers with real ceilings before pick 55, and it let him sit on quarterback until the seventh. Jayden Daniels at #79 was the best value of the entire draft, a QB5 at a QB13 price, and then he came back in the twelfth for Brock Purdy as insurance nobody else bothered to buy. Kenneth Walker III and Bucky Irving anchor the backfield with Rico Dowdle behind them at a two-point discount.
The one thing to watch is the running back room, which grades out coolest of the four — though Dowdle, Kenny Gainwell and Brian Robinson Jr. give him three lottery tickets and waivers exist. Adam is 34-22 with no losing season ever, and this is what quietly relentless looks like on paper.

copies.headline: Peter Built A Wide Receiver Fortress
copies.body:
Start with Bijan Robinson at 1.02 and never look back. Peter turned the next three rounds into a receiving room most teams can't match: A.J. Brown at WR8 for a +3 discount, George Pickens, then Tee Higgins in the fourth as a +4 value. That's three top-20 receivers before round five. Then he waited on quarterback and got paid — Lamar Jackson at pick 50, a +17 steal and the best value of his draft, backed up by Dak Prescott in the 13th at +30. Tucker Kraft gives him a real TE7 anchor. The A grades at QB and WR are earned.
The one thing to watch is the RB room behind Bijan, where the Jordan Mason pick at #95 is the biggest reach of the entire draft. But he took five swings back there, and Bijan's Week 11 bye is the only real hole to plug.
Peter's 2022 title still sets the league record. This roster looks like a man who remembers.

copies.headline: The Aura Farm Builds a Real Contender
copies.body:
Christian opened with CeeDee Lamb at 11 and never wobbled off the plan. The receiver room is the best thing he owns — Lamb, DeVonta Smith at pick 38 for +3 in value, Jameson Williams in the sixth, then Khalil Shakir and Deebo Samuel as WR4 and WR5 depth most rosters would start. The backfield came fast and deep: Chase Brown in the second, Travis Etienne in the third, Bhayshul Tuten in the fifth, with Aaron Jones and Dylan Sampson behind them. And he waited on quarterback perfectly, taking Trevor Lawrence in the seventh at +2 and then stealing Jordan Love in the 14th at +21, the steal of his draft.
The one thing to watch is tight end, where George Kittle in the eighth was the aggressive move, but Kittle is Kittle and Chig Okonkwo is a fine week-to-week fallback. Boom-or-bust incarnate — 10-4 then 4-10 — and this is the roster that finally makes the boom the default setting.

copies.headline: Two Elite Backs, A Quarterback Steal
copies.body:
Noah walked in knowing exactly what he wanted and left with it. James Cook III and De'Von Achane as the RB5/RB7 pairing gives him the highest-floor backfield in this room, and Achane at #17 came in four spots of value above cost. Then the real coup: Drake Maye as QB3 in round five, a +15 value swing and the steal of his draft. Colston Loveland at TE3 in the fourth means he's got top-shelf production at three of four positions, which is a hard thing to say about anybody. Rhamondre Stevenson in the seventh is legitimate insurance and legitimate upside at RB27.
The one thing to watch is the receiver room, where Garrett Wilson and Mike Evans headline a group short on certainty — but Michael Wilson came in at +10 value and there are fourteen weeks of waivers to sort it out. And nobody wants Noah in round one anyway: five playoff wins and a 2024 title from the 7 seed.

copies.headline: Elite Receivers, Hurts At Cost, Real Structure
copies.body:
Logan built this from the outside in and it works. Justin Jefferson at 10 is the safest anchor in the sport, and the WR room behind him — Tetairoa McMillan, Luther Burden III, Michael Pittman Jr., Xavier Worthy, Rashid Shaheed — is stacked six deep with actual upside instead of filler. Saquon Barkley in the second gives the backfield a genuine RB1, and Jeremiyah Love at 34 was the steal of his draft, a +7 value at RB15. Then he waited on quarterback and got Jalen Hurts in the sixth, another +7, a top-six QB at a price that let him spend everywhere else first. That's a plan, executed.
The one thing to watch is tight end, where Isaiah Likely in the ninth was his worst pick, but TE is the position waivers solve fastest and he has the WR depth to trade from. As for the owner: two #1 seeds, one dress, still the most dangerous roster-builder in the room. This is the year the curse looks stupid.

copies.headline: Kaleb Built Around Youth And Waited On Quarterback
copies.body:
The plan was legible from pick one: get the young guys with the biggest workloads and let the rest come to you. Ashton Jeanty and Breece Hall — Hall at RB13 in the third, a genuine value — give him a backfield with real ceiling, and Drake London and Ladd McConkey are the kind of WR7/WR17 anchors you don't have to think about again. Then the patience paid. Justin Herbert in the eighth at QB8 was the steal of his draft, and coming back for Jared Goff in the fourteenth at QB16 was a +30 flourish. Harold Fannin Jr. headlines a tight end room that graded out an A.
The one thing to watch is the RB depth behind the top two, though RJ Harvey in the ninth was a +6 swing at exactly that. The original Cinderella has turned three straight 8-6 seasons into a habit; this looks like the roster that finally breaks the pattern upward.

copies.headline: A Deep Backfield And A Bargain Quarterback
copies.body:
CJ built this thing from the ground floor out. Jonathan Taylor at #9 was RB4 off the board at a slight discount, and then he just kept stacking backs — Quinshon Judkins, TreVeyon Henderson, Chuba Hubbard, Isiah Pacheco, Zach Charbonnet. That's five running backs behind an anchor, which means injuries and bye weeks are somebody else's problem. Then he sat on quarterback until round 6 and got Joe Burrow as QB4, a +16 value and the steal of his draft. Waiting worked. Tyler Shough at #160 as a +27 value is a free swing behind him.
The one thing to watch is tight end, where Jake Ferguson at TE12 is the floor rather than the ceiling — but that's the position you stream, and CJ has the RB depth to trade from. For a guy who's spent four years one break short of the bracket, this is the most coherent roster he's built. Leif's 4-4 with him for a reason.

copies.headline: Two Elite Tight Ends and a Plan
copies.body:
John walked in with a vision and executed it: get the best players at the positions where the drop-off is steepest. Puka Nacua in the first, then Brock Bowers and Trey McBride back-to-back — McBride at +6 value in the third is a room nobody else in this league can match, and having two top-two tight ends means one of them is a weekly matchup problem in the flex. Then he let running back come to him and got Kyren Williams at #45, twelve spots of value and the steal of his draft. Matthew Stafford in the 13th at +30 behind Caleb Williams is a free lottery ticket at a position he'd already solved.
The one thing to watch is the RB room behind Kyren, but Blake Corum, Tyrone Tracy and Keaton Mitchell are exactly the kind of cheap swings that turn into starters by Week 5. Fitting for the older Lundquist — 6-3 on Peter, 10-4 last year, still hunting the ring — to draft like a man who knows what he's doing.

copies.headline: Gibbs At One, Kelce In Ten
copies.body:
Mitchell took Jahmyr Gibbs with the first overall pick and then built a roster that actually complements him. Josh Jacobs behind Gibbs gives him a two-back floor most teams in this league can't match, and Nico Collins at 24 is a legitimate WR1 anchor. The tight end room is the real triumph: Tyler Warren as the TE4 off the board, then Travis Kelce at pick 120 — the steal of his draft at plus-13 — which means he can start one and trade from surplus. Alvin Kamara in round 16 at plus-26 is a free swing with actual name-brand upside, and Courtland Sutton and DJ Moore give the receiver room proven bodies.
The one thing to watch is quarterback, with Jaxson Dart in round six, but Daniel Jones at 168 came in as value and the position turns over on waivers faster than any other. Fitting for the human coin flip: three 7-7 seasons, two playoff wins, and now a roster with a spine.

copies.headline: Grant Built A Wide Receiver Fortress
copies.body:
The plan here was never subtle: get elite at one position and dominate it. Amon-Ra St. Brown at 1.6 is the anchor, then Zay Flowers, Jaylen Waddle, Christian Watson and Chris Godwin behind him — that's an A-grade receiver room by any benchmark, five deep, and it's why this roster has a real ceiling. Omarion Hampton at RB10 in the second is the value pick that keeps the backfield honest, and the late rounds were his sharpest work: Dallas Goedert (+4), Juwan Johnson (+11), and Baker Mayfield in the 13th at +22, the steal of his draft. Waiting on quarterback that long and landing a starter is exactly how you're supposed to do it.
The one thing to watch is the backfield depth behind Hampton, but Tony Pollard, Tank Bigsby and Jacory Croskey-Merritt are all lottery tickets that cost him nothing, and one hitting solves it. Fitting for Grant: 3-11, then 9-5, then 5-9, and a 5-4 lead over Logan in the chaos derby. Nobody predicts him. That's the point.

copies.headline: A Receiver Room Built To Bully
copies.body:
Isaac walked in with a plan and never blinked: Ja'Marr Chase at 1.03, Malik Nabers in the third, Terry McLaurin in the fourth, DK Metcalf in the sixth. That's an A-grade wide receiver room with four legitimate weekly anchors, and in a league where everyone else is scrambling for a WR3, he'll be starting guys other teams would flex. Cam Skattebo at 5.51 came in ahead of consensus, Jaylen Warren adds a real backfield floor next to Javonte Williams, and Dalton Kincaid at 12.142 was a +17 steal of his draft. Then Bo Nix in the tenth at +24 — his best value pick, and proof that waiting on quarterback works when you know which one you want.
The one thing to watch is the backfield, but Skattebo and Warren both carry standalone value and waivers will churn running backs by October. Isaac started 11-3 in 2022 and has been chasing that high ever since. This is the roster that gets him back there.

copies.headline: Leif Built a Backfield Nobody Wants To Face
copies.body:
Leif walked in with a plan and refused to blink: Christian McCaffrey at 1.05, Derrick Henry in the second, David Montgomery in the fifth. That's an A-grade running back room in a league where everyone else spends the middle rounds praying. Then he got Josh Allen at pick 29, nine spots past market, the steal of his draft, and doubled back in round 13 for Patrick Mahomes at a +30 discount — the QB1 and a former MVP for the price of one. Kyle Pitts Sr. gives him a legitimate tight end edge. The Davante Adams and Marvin Harrison Jr. combination is real upside at the top of the receiver room.
The one thing to watch is wideout depth, but Jayden Reed and Stefon Diggs are two names nobody's dropping for free, and waivers exist for a reason. Four years of Joey Lunchbox loyalty, 22-34, and this is the first roster that looks built to make CJ nervous in that 4-4 series.

intro: Five drafts into this thing and the cabin has never produced a board this clean — nobody walked away from Players Weekend with a roster they had to apologize for. Adam did Adam things, turning the Uncut Cokerr into the only A on the sheet, with Peter, Christian and Noah right behind him at A- and each one built on a completely different premise. The tight end run in the fifth and sixth was the one genuine stampede of the weekend, and the guys who sat it out came away with backfields deep enough to make it look intentional. From Logan's B+ down to Leif's C+, this is less a ranking than a list of teams that are going to be annoying to play in November.
